title: Ocean and Atmosphere Circulation
seo_title: Grade 6 Climate Worksheets: Unequal Heating, Global Winds and Ocean Currents
standard_text: Develop and use a model to describe how unequal heating and rotation of the Earth cause patterns of atmospheric and oceanic circulation that determine regional climates.
meta_desc: Free middle school science worksheets on ocean and atmosphere circulation (NGSS MS-ESS2-6): unequal heating, convection and global winds, ocean currents like the Gulf Stream, and regional climates. 100 practice questions with answers.
key_big: Unequal heating and Earth's spin move air and water.
key_sub: These moving winds and ocean currents carry heat around Earth and shape the climate of each region.
body_html:
How to think about it

Earth is heated unequally: sunlight hits the equator directly and the poles at a slant, so the equator gets more energy per area.

Unequal heating makes air and water move. Warm air rises and cool air sinks, forming convection cells and global winds. Earth's rotation makes winds and currents curve. Winds push the ocean surface into currents: warm currents (like the Gulf Stream) carry heat toward the poles, and cold currents (like the California Current) cool coasts.

Together with mountains and oceans, these patterns create regional climates.

Example

Why is it warmer at the equator?

Sunlight hits it directly.

Answer: It gets more concentrated energy from the sun.

Example

How does the Gulf Stream affect England?

It is a warm current.

Answer: It keeps winters milder.

Common mistakes

  • Thinking the equator is hotter because it is closer to the sun.
  • Thinking warm air sinks.
  • Forgetting that oceans carry heat and affect the climate on land.

faq.a: Sunlight hits the equator directly and the poles at a slant, so the equator gets more energy per area.
Mostly winds blowing over the ocean, along with differences in temperature and Earth's rotation.

faq.q: How do ocean currents affect climate?
faq.a: Warm currents carry heat toward the poles and warm nearby land; cold currents cool nearby coasts.

items.q: Ravi completes the sentence: “Cold air at the poles ____.”
c: moves in a straight line no matter what
rises, because it is less dense
moves from high pressure toward low pressure
sinks, because it is more dense
items.e: Cold air at the poles sinks, because it is more dense.

items.q: Ben shines a flashlight straight down and then at a slant onto graph paper. The slanted light covers more squares and is dimmer. What does this model?
c: Sunlight is spread out near the poles, so they get less energy per area.
The poles are farther from the sun.
items.e: The angle of sunlight explains unequal heating.

items.q: Why do coastal areas have milder temperatures than inland areas?
c: Water heats up and cools down more slowly than land.
The ocean makes its own heat.
items.e: Large bodies of water moderate climate.

items.q: How do warm ocean currents affect nearby land?
c: They make the climate warmer and often wetter.
items.e: The ocean shares its heat with the air.

items.q: Ruby asks why the equator is the warmest part of Earth on average. What is the best explanation?

items.e: Unequal heating comes from the angle of sunlight, not the distance to the sun.

The warm Gulf Stream flows toward Western Europe.
items.e: Ocean currents carry heat.

items.q: Emma reads that the Labrador Current flows south from the Arctic along the coast of Canada. Is it a warm or a cold current?
c: a current of air, not water
items.e: Currents that flow from near the equator toward the poles are warm; currents from the poles are cold.

items.q: Lily compares London, England (near the Gulf Stream) and Calgary, Canada (inland, about as far north). Which has milder winters?
items.e: The warm Gulf Stream keeps London's winters mild.

items.q: Owen compares San Francisco (on the coast) and Sacramento (inland). Which has a smaller difference between summer and winter temperatures?
items.e: The ocean warms and cools slowly, so coastal places have milder temperatures.

subject: science
